layer: retrieval corpus (one card per model card, plus the results, the tables and the narrative)

chunking.split_rule: Markdown documents split on H2 headings, except when a document has no H2 (then the whole body is one chunk). The document's H1 and the section heading are prepended to every chunk so a retrieved fragment carries its own title. Any text over the budget — a section *or* a model card — splits on blank-line paragraph boundaries, keeping tables whole where they fit; a single block longer than the budget is split on sentence ends. Parts after the first are ided `<chunk_id>#p2`, `<chunk_id>#p3`, and every part opens with a one-line prefix naming the parent document and its part number, so a part retrieved on its own is still identifiable.
chunking.merge_rule: A tail fragment shorter than min_chars is merged back into the previous chunk of the same section rather than shipped as a header with no body. The exception is a chunk that is already at max_chars, which is left as is: merging would break the budget the embedding model was declared with.
chunking.determinism: Chunk ids depend only on the source path and the anchor, never on iteration order or a timestamp, so a rebuild over unchanged sources produces identical ids and identical text. The manifest's `generated_at` is the only field allowed to change.
chunking.text_normalisation: Line endings are normalised to `\n` and trailing whitespace stripped. Nothing else is altered: markdown emphasis is left in place because the answer layer renders it and because stripping it would make the chunk's text differ from the document it cites.

retrieval.baseline: BM25 (k1=1.5, b=0.75) over the same chunks, dependency-free
retrieval.baseline_why: The lexical baseline exists so the embedding numbers have something to beat. If BM25 retrieves the gold chunk as often as the embeddings do, the corpus is keyword-addressable and the model is not adding anything — a fact that should be measured rather than assumed, and one this project's chunk sizes make plausible.

refusal_rule.out_of_scope: Refuse when the top-1 similarity is below `0.5 x the median top-1 similarity of the answerable eval questions`, **or** when the top-1 chunk is `scope:answer`. The threshold is scale-free and is calibrated on the eval set, which makes refusal recall optimistic; the artifact publishes the threshold, the median it came from and that caveat. BM25 scores are not comparable to cosine, so the baseline reports retrieval only and does not make a refusal decision.
refusal_rule.refusal_with_reason: **Not a score decision at all.** A question the data cannot answer should retrieve the passage that says why with *high* similarity — that is the point of putting the limitations page in the corpus. So this type is measured by whether the reason chunk is in the top 5, and the answer is required to cite it; using "low similarity" as the test here would score a well-argued refusal as a failure.
refusal_rule.measured: The first build made exactly that mistake: one score threshold was applied to both kinds of refusal and reported 0 of 2 reason-bearing questions as "refused" while the reason chunk was ranked first. The two rules are separate because the two questions are different questions.

source_hash_rule: sha256 of each source with CRLF normalised to LF — the same bytes the git index stores under .gitattributes (eol=lf), so a Windows checkout and the Linux runner hash identically

sources.hash_rule: sha256 of the file with CRLF normalised to LF (the index's eol=lf)

chunks.title: Data coverage — the Stage 3 quality gate result
chunks.text:
Stage 3 gated 672 series at report vintage 2026-10-18: 357 ok, 313 flagged and 2 empty.

Study window: starts 1999-01-01, ends the latest observation. The first administration under study begins 1999-05-29 (Obasanjo). Data before that describes a different exchange-rate and fiscal regime and cannot inform any estimate this project makes.

Thresholds: gap gate flags more than 3 missing months; the spike gate flags a move beyond 50.0 percent (or 10.0 percentage points for series already in percent); the revision tolerance is 1.0 percent.

A flag is not a deletion: the series remains in the base with its status travelling on it. The share of the monthly spine that is actually observed, and what each flag means, are in docs/limitations.md.
chunks.citation: Data coverage — the Stage 3 quality gate result — registry/quality/2026-10-18/report.json (vintage 2026-10-18)

chunks.title: Registry coverage — how many cards carry a published number
chunks.text: The registry holds 36 model cards: 12 outcomes across 3 identification designs. 2 cards carry a published estimate and 34 carry a reason instead, from a closed set: design_not_run 3; design_result_is_channel_level 9; no_specification_declared 10; outcome_series_absent 12. A card with no number is not a null result — it names why no specification was published for that (outcome, design) pair. The design-level results (the national FAAC channel and Design C's non-run) sit on the index, once, because they are statements about the channel a design rests on rather than about any single card's outcome.
chunks.citation: Registry coverage — how many cards carry a published number — registry/dags/index.json (vintage 2026-10-18)

[data-dictionary — `dim_administration` and `dim_ — part 1 of 3]

`dim_administration` is the base spec §7 table unchanged — five rows, one per president, including the two
rows that cover two terms. `end_date_effective` is the **half-open** span bound: four boundaries have
`end_date` equal to the next `start_date`, one has a one-day gap (Yar'Adua 2010-05-05, Jonathan sworn

[data-dictionary — `faac_national_monthly` — part 2 of 2]

**Three decisions this artifact encodes** (S6-03, S6-04, and the parse report): the month is

anywhere (81 of them, 6 inside the study window, none after 2009-11) is **absent** rather than zero,

chunks.title: data-dictionary — Vintage and provenance conventions
chunks.text:
Data dictionary — the analytical base

## Vintage and provenance conventions

- Every fact and dimension row carries the raw `vintage` it came from. Only the latest vintage per source
  is read (`stg_raw_manifest` is the single place that decides), so `worldbank/2026-10-10` — retained on
  disk for revision detection — cannot leak into the base. A dbt test fails if it ever does.
- `vintage_date` = ingest date; corrections create a **new vintage**, never an edit (X-07).
- The Stage 3 report vintage travels as `quality_vintage`, and the verifier fails if a carried
  `quality_status` disagrees with the report it claims to come from.
- `declared_in_vintage` on `dim_definition_break` names the report the annotation came from.

chunks.title: Transition event study — what it does not claim
chunks.text:
What the transition event study does not claim:
- A causal effect of a tenure, a party or a president on conflict. The design is a within-series timing comparison and nothing here identifies a counterfactual.
- That conflict is measured without reporting bias. UCDP GED is a reported-events archive; the divergence check is a guard, not a fix.
- A pooled 'tenure effect'. Four event-level estimates are published; there is no average.
- Anything about the annual outcome domains. They have no monthly series, which is the same wall Stage 5 hit.

The party split is published as description with no test (no_test_computed: true), because two events against two events carries no sampling distribution.
chunks.citation: Transition event study — what it does not claim — registry/events/2026-10-18/events.json (vintage 2026-10-18)

A card carries: the outcome and its coverage status, the design and its estimator, the node/edge

chunks.title: dags — Coverage is not the same as identifiability
chunks.text:
verify (independent of R: re-derives acyclicity and the backdoor-blocking property)

## Coverage is not the same as identifiability

A graph is a claim about causal structure; it is valid whether or not the outcome series currently
reaches the study window. All 12 catalogue outcomes therefore have all three graphs, with coverage
carried alongside on the card:

- **Health** — usable (interpolated annual series).
- **Economy** — usable (note the 2014 rebasing break).
- **Education** — `declared_gap`: no open outcome series reaches the APC tenures. The graphs exist;
  the card says the data do not.
- **Security** — `blocked`: depends entirely on ACLED/UCDP, not yet wired.

"We found no education effect" and "we had no post-2010 education outcome" are different statements.
Only the second is true here, and the card carries the distinction.

[dags — Every variable, and where it comes from — part 5 of 13]

That matters here rather than in a footnote: `donor` sits in the adjustment set for **design A and
design B on every health and education outcome**, so conditioning on it partially conditions on a debt
restructuring that coincided with the start of the 2003–2007 tenure. Stage 5 must annotate those cards

This is the intended division of labour: the graph layer declares *what is held fixed*, and the quality
gates record *whether that thing is fit to hold fixed* (decisions C-28). ### Still missing, by root cause

chunks.title: dags — How "assumed absent" is computed and shown
chunks.text:
verify (independent of R: re-derives acyclicity and the backdoor-blocking property)

## How "assumed absent" is computed and shown

Each design includes exactly one **unobserved** node. The graph displayed includes it, drawn and
labelled `(assumed absent)`. The adjustment set, however, is computed by `dagitty` on the
**assumed graph** — unobserved nodes and their edges removed — with `type = "minimal"` and
`effect = "total"`. The full graph is not identifiable (an unblockable backdoor path runs through
the unobserved node), which is precisely the point: the estimate is *conditional on that node being
absent*, and the card states it rather than burying it.
chunks.citation: dags — How "assumed absent" is computed and shown — docs/dags.md (vintage 2026-10-18)

## The question, and the exposure

The question is the influence of a **regime / administration** on outcomes in health, security,
education and the economy. The exposure is therefore always the administration. The three designs
differ in how the exposure is operationalised:

| Design | How the administration enters | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| **A** — State dose-response DiD | A federal policy shift, with each state's exposure intensity as the dose | state-month |
| **B** — National VECM / ARDL | The party×tenure dummy, interacted with oil | national-month |
| **C** — Synthetic control | The treated tenure itself, against a donor pool | country-year |

## The three designs, as assumptions

[dags — The three designs, as assumptions — part 1 of 4]

### A — State dose-response DiD
**Estimand:** ATT of a federal policy shift, with state exposure as the dose.
**Adjustment set:** `{inherit, oil, statefe, timefe}` — plus `donor` for health and education.
**Identifying assumption:** parallel trends — absent the shift, states with different exposure would
have followed parallel paths; formally, no unmeasured state-by-time confounder drives both dose and
outcome. The unobserved node `u_st` is assumed absent.
**Does not establish:** anticipation before the formal date; SUTVA violations via cross-state
spillovers; that the dose itself is uncontaminated by the policy it measures.

## The three designs, as assumptions

[dags — The three designs, as assumptions — part 2 of 4]

### B — National VECM / ARDL time series
**Estimand:** the long-run multiplier for the administration effect, oil-interacted.
**Adjustment set:** `{oil}`.
**Identifying assumption:** conditional exogeneity of the administration dummy given oil, lagged
outcome, fiscal and FX controls and the trend. The unobserved node `u_t` is assumed absent.
**Does not establish:** the *total* effect — `faac` and `fx` are downstream of the administration,
so conditioning on them identifies a **direct effect net of the fiscal and FX channel**. Also:
~26 annual observations, five administrations, wide intervals; structural breaks not fully absorbed.

## The three designs, as assumptions

[dags — The three designs, as assumptions — part 4 of 4]

### C — Synthetic control (cross-country)
**Estimand:** the treatment gap, Nigeria minus synthetic Nigeria.
**Adjustment set:** `{common}`.
**Identifying assumption:** the donor-weighted common factors (above all the oil cycle) stand in for
Nigeria's counterfactual, and no Nigeria-specific shock coincides with the treatment. The unobserved
node `u_ng` is assumed absent.
**Does not establish:** anything when pre-treatment fit is weak, or when an idiosyncratic
Nigeria-only shock falls inside the window. Where the donor pool cannot produce a credible
counterfactual, the card says so instead of shipping the gap.

Design memo — what the data can support (Stage 5)

## 1. The grain the tests run on

[design-memo — 1. The grain the tests run on — part 1 of 2]

Every test runs on the **native observation** a source actually published — never on the monthly
spine. The spine used by the app is only **16.2 % observed** (1,349 of 8,350 rows; 4,389 interpolated,
2,612 empty — it was 10.1 % of 7,682 before the monthly Brent, FAAC and UCDP landings). A unit-root or
cointegration test on interpolated rows reports the properties of the interpolator, not of the data:
linear interpolation induces near-perfect serial correlation by construction, so ADF would fail to reject
stationarity for a series that is strongly mean-reverting, and Johansen would find rank in a system of
straight lines.

## 3. Family B — national VECM / ARDL — **degraded**

[design-memo — 3. Family B — national VECM / ARDL — part 2 of 11]

Each series is classified I(0) / I(1) / I(2) only when all three tests agree at the level **and** at
the first difference. A single level-regime break (Brent 2008; the naira 2016 and 2023) must not be
read as a second unit root. Where the three tests disagree the series is carried as **I(1)** —the conservative branch, which can only make the reported cointegration rank smaller — and the card marks
it inconclusive. **10 of the 18 testable series are inconclusive** (`I(1)*` in the report; the other 8
of the 26 are too short to test at all); that is an honest reading of ~26 annual observations, not noise
to be averaged away. ### 3.2 Cointegration (Johansen, `{Y, log(oil), fx}`, K=2)

A rank equal to the system dimension means the trace test rejected every rank below it — the system
simply reads as *stationary*, which is not cointegration, so the honest estimator is a VAR in levels

[design-memo — 3. Family B — national VECM / ARDL — part 5 of 11]

**A caveat the verifier found, recorded rather than buried.** `urca::ca.jo` and an independent

under that difference for five of six outcomes; for **`mmr` it is not** — the deciding statistic sits

3. `mmr`'s Design B card carries `rank marginal` in the check detail; Stage 6 must not treat its

## 3. Family B — national VECM / ARDL — **degraded**

[design-memo — 3. Family B — national VECM / ARDL — part 8 of 11]

Written down **before** any estimate, per PHASES.md. The Tier-3 MDE of **35–99 residual SDs** looks
absurd until it is separated from the data: dropping the mandated `oil × tenure` interactions (the
"leaner" column) brings it to **1.8–5.9 SD**. **The interaction terms alone widen the detectable
effect ~10–20×**, because they are nearly collinear with the tenure dummies themselves (R² 0.997–0.999).
That is a statement about the *design matrix*, not about the data — the base spec makes the
interaction non-negotiable (M-03), and it is what makes a ~23-row annual design unable to detect
anything short of a huge effect. Stage 6 must report the interval, never the point, and this table is
why.

[design-memo — 4. Family C — synthetic control —  — part 1 of 10]

**Re-run 2026-10-18** against a **99-country** candidate pool screened on oil dependence, region/income

chunks.text:
Design memo — what the data can support (Stage 5)

## 5. Shock-window visibility

[design-memo — 5. Shock-window visibility — part 2 of 2]

Brent is genuinely monthly and complete, so each shock is **visible on `oil`**. But on the annual
outcomes the window is measured by **one** observed point (the July anchor), and inside the 2023
window the other months are interpolated. Any claim about what happened *inside* such a window is a
claim about that one anchor month. This is the same constraint as §1 seen from the shock side, and it
is why the 2023 window is not monthly-visible on the landed CPI.

chunks.title: design-memo — 6. What was dropped, on the record
chunks.text:
Design memo — what the data can support (Stage 5)

## 6. What was dropped, on the record

- **Family A** — dropped. PHASES.md Stage 5 dose validation: a dose with near-zero cross-state
  variance cannot support a dose-response design, and no estimator fixes that. (0 of 12,358 values.)
- **Family C** — feasible on `u5mr` only (re-run 2026-10-18 over a 99-country pool): 3 of its 4 windows
  pass the pre-fit gate, `gdp_growth` passes 1 of 4 and `cpi_yoy` none. No candidate treated window lets any convex combination of the donors
  track Nigeria's pre-treatment path. Reported infeasible rather than estimated, per the Stage 6 gate.
- **Family B** — degraded, not dropped. It can be estimated, but at annual grain and without FAAC, and
  with a ~38–99 SD detectable effect on the Tier-3 design. The deviations are named on every card.

---

chunks.title: design-memo — 7. What this hands to Stage 6
chunks.text:
Design memo — what the data can support (Stage 5)

## 7. What this hands to Stage 6

1. **Nothing clears its gate**, so Stage 6 does not estimate a headline effect. It estimates the
   *boundary*: what an annual Design B VECM/ARDL, and the narrower differenced Synthetic Control,
   can and cannot say — with the MDE table as the disclaimer.
2. **The single unblocking action** is the NBS FAAC parser (a PDF/HTML parser in the same family as the
   monthly NBS CPI parse). It revives Family A outright and restores the base-spec Tier-3 system for
   Family B.
3. **`mmr`'s Design B rank is marginal** and must not be reported as settled.
4. **Every point estimate carries its interval**, and a multiplier whose interval spans both signs is
   not a finding (PHASES.md Stage 6).

## 8. How to reproduce

```bash
Rscript analysis/R/02_diagnostics.R                    # writes diagnostics.json + report.md
```

one outcome** (re-run 2026-10-18) | pre-treatment fit over a **99-country** pool: `u5mr` passes **3 of its 4** windows; `gdp_growth` 1 of 4 and `cpi_yoy` 0 of 4 do not pass the declared strict-majority rollup | build the estimator and its placebos on the `u5mr` windows |

What this project can actually answer

## 1. The presidential-tenure question is not answerable, and no estimator makes it so

[estimates — 1. The presidential-tenure question  — part 3 of 3]

Read the first column: the design could only detect a tenure effect *as large as the series' own
residual variation*. A mortality rate moving by its entire residual standard deviation because a
president changed is not a hypothesis, it is a placeholder. Sub-national monthly grain is the only way
out of it, and three of the four outcome domains have no sub-national monthly series at all
(`docs/data-dictionary.md`, declared gaps).

So: **any "Buhari caused X" or "the APC did Y" number this project could produce would be a restatement
of its own assumptions.** That is not a null result, and the project does not report it as one.

## 2. What the data *can* carry is the fiscal channel — and that is what landed after Stage 5

[estimates — 2. What the data *can* carry is the  — part 11 of 16]

**A 10 % rise in Brent reaches the states as roughly a 5 % larger allocation, two to three months
later.** The lag is what the disbursement calendar implies rather than a curiosity: the allocation
published for a month is revenue accrued in an earlier one, so an immediate response would have been the
surprising result. The lead placebo — regressing today's allocation on a *future* oil shock — is
+0.095 (SE 0.152), an order of magnitude smaller than the peak response at h = 2.

## 2. What the data *can* carry is the fiscal channel — and that is what landed after Stage 5

[estimates — 2. What the data *can* carry is the  — part 4 of 16]

* **A mis-timed dose is as good as the timed one.** Refitting the same estimator with each state's dose
  series shifted by any non-zero offset from −30 to +30 months, **8 of 60 offsets return an estimate at
  least as large** as the estimate itself (p = 0.133). The deterministic 24-month placebo returns
  **+0.302** against the estimate's **+0.479**. * **The identifying variation is a commodity price.** What survives state and month fixed effects in the
  dose is concentrated in the oil-producing states: residual sd **0.50 in Delta, 0.50 in Bayelsa, 0.47 in
  Rivers** against **0.11** in Sokoto, Bauchi, Adamawa, Kaduna and Taraba.

What this project can actually answer

## 3. The answer, in one paragraph

[estimates — 3. The answer, in one paragraph — part 1 of 2]

**Of the four questions this project set out to answer, one is not answerable (presidential tenure
effects on national annual outcomes), one is now estimable but not identified (does federal money reduce
local violence), and one is answerable and answered (an oil-price shock reaches Nigeria's states with an
elasticity of roughly 0.5 at a two-to-three-month lag).** The fourth — synthetic control against a donor
pool — cleared its pre-fit gate on one outcome once the pool was widened (2026-10-18) and now waits on an
estimator rather than on data. **A fifth question turned out to be answerable and is answered: did
conflict move inside each tenure?** (`docs/events.md`: two of eight event-outcome cells survive both the
placebo and the pre-trend check.)

## 1. Why this and not a tenure comparison

[events — 1. Why this and not a tenure comparison — part 1 of 2]

| What the question wants | Why this design cannot give it |
|---|---|
| "Was violence lower under tenure A than tenure B?" | Two tenures are two numbers at a national grain. Comparing them is a comparison of two means with no variance: there is no counterfactual, and annual data gives 2-4 points per tenure |
| "Did the transition *cause* the change?" | The Indian Ocean is not a control group. The transition is simultaneous with the appointment of a government, a security budget, an amnesty and an offensive |
| What it *can* say | "Reported fatalities in the 12 months after this transition were X % different from the 96 months before it, and that is larger/smaller than the same statistic at the 58 months where no transition happened" |
chunks.citation: events — 1. Why this and not a tenure comparison — docs/events.md (vintage 2026-10-18)

## 1. Why this and not a tenure comparison

[events — 1. Why this and not a tenure comparison — part 2 of 2]

The design's binding constraint is stated up front and never relaxed: **four events**. Inference is by
**exhaustive placebo assignment** — every eligible month is tried as if it were a transition, with the same
windows, statistic and controls — rather than by a t-statistic that would assume four independent draws.

[events — 2. The series and the events — part 1 of 3]

- **312 months**, 1999-01 → 2024-12, UCDP GED national monthly counts (fatalities and incidents).

## 3. Windows and the statistic

[events — 3. Windows and the statistic — part 1 of 2]

- **Pre-window: 96 months**, the same for every event, so the four estimates are the same calculation. - **Post windows: 12 and 24 months**, truncated at the successor transition and at the end of the series. - **Floor: 75 % of the requested horizon** (9 of 12 months, 18 of 24). A window below the floor is published
  as `not_estimated` with its reason and the months it had; it is never fitted, and no cell is silently
  dropped. Tinubu's 20-month h=24 window clears the floor and is published **with its truncation flag**. - **Statistic**: Poisson ML on the count, `count ~ post + factor(month_of_year) + trend`, Newey-West (HAC)
  standard errors at 12 lags, reported as `exp(beta) - 1` — the proportional monthly shift over the post
  window.

## 4. Inference: the placebo is the null, and it is enumerated

[events — 4. Inference: the placebo is the null,  — part 1 of 3]

Every eligible month — one with 96 months of history before it, enough after it, and **more than 24 months
from any real transition** — is treated as if it were a transition. 58 months (2012-06 → 2021-04) qualify.
The set is **enumerated, not sampled**: no random number generator is involved, so there is no seed and the
engine and the verifier compute the same distribution from the same data. Two properties of that null shape how the results must be read:

Comparing tenures, part 1 — what changed *inside* a tenure

## 4. Inference: the placebo is the null, and it is enumerated

[events — 4. Inference: the placebo is the null,  — part 2 of 3]

- **It is not centred on zero.** Placebo mean for fatalities at h=12 is −0.390 (a 32 % *decline*): reported
  violence drifts down through the window, so the typical month already looks like a fall.
- The p-value is therefore the **tail the estimate points at** — for a rise, the share of placebos at least
  as large; for a fall, at least as small — in the add-one form `(1 + #{tail}) / (n + 1)`. It is never zero:
  with 58 placebo months the smallest attainable value is 1/59 = 0.017, and the artifact may not claim more
  resolution than that.

chunks.text:
Comparing tenures, part 1 — what changed *inside* a tenure

## 6. The party split is a description, and the artifact enforces that

| Party | Events | Median h=12 shift (fatalities) | The shifts |
|---|---|---|---|
| PDP | 2 | +55.3 % | −17.1 %, +127.7 % |
| APC | 2 | +4.6 % | −67.5 %, +76.6 % |

**No test statistic is computed**, because two events against two events has no sampling distribution and
any p-value would be a number manufactured by an assumption. `party_split.no_test_computed` is `true`, the
JSON Schema requires it to be `true`, and `tests/verify_events.py` fails if a p-value, standard error or
t-statistic field appears anywhere inside that block. The four values above are published so the reader can
see what a two-against-two comparison would be made of.

chunks.text:
Comparing tenures, part 1 — what changed *inside* a tenure

## 9. What this unlocks, and what it does not

Start here when someone asks to compare tenures, and expect to say: on monthly conflict, two of eight
event-outcome cells show a shift that survives the pre-trend check, three fail it, one shows no shift, and
two cannot be checked at all. On everything else — health, education, the economy — there is no monthly
series, so the only route to a tenure-level statement remains a counterfactual, which is the donor-pool
problem Stage 5 left open (`docs/design-memo.md`, Design C).

## 1. The question this project was asked is not answerable with this data

[limitations — 1. The question this project was a — part 3 of 4]

The Tier-3 column is not a quirk of the estimator; it is the mandated `oil × tenure` interactions, which
are collinear with the tenure dummies at R² 0.997–0.999. The only effects this design can see are ones as
large as the series' own residual variation, which is not a hypothesis. **This is a statement about
arithmetic, not a null result**, and the distinction matters: "we found no tenure effect" would imply the
design could have found one.

## 2. Most of the monthly spine is not observed

[limitations — 2. Most of the monthly spine is no — part 1 of 2]

The analytical base holds **8,350 rows** (25 metrics × 334 months). Of those, **1,349 rows (16.2 %) are
observed**, 4,389 are interpolated and 2,612 are unobserved. The monthly series the app draws is
therefore a picture of the interpolation rule in most cells, which is why the base carries
`observation_type` on every row and why the app must render interpolated segments dashed.
chunks.citation: limitations — 2. Most of the monthly spine is not observed — docs/limitations.md (vintage 2026-10-18)

chunks.text:
What this project cannot say — the limitations, written before the findings

## 2. Most of the monthly spine is not observed

[limitations — 2. Most of the monthly spine is no — part 2 of 2]

- **Tests never run on the spine.** Every unit-root, cointegration, pre-fit and power test runs on the
  native grain a source published (S5-01). A test on interpolated rows reports the interpolator's
  serial correlation as if it were the data's.
- **Three frequency gaps are declared, not smoothed:** `cpi_yoy`, `gdp_growth`, `unemp`. The CPI series is
  annual, which is why the 2023 subsidy-removal window is **not monthly-visible** even though the spine
  now reaches it (C-30). A monthly VECM on `cpi_yoy` would estimate the interpolation.
- **Consequence for Design B:** its testable system is the annual cross-check, ~26 observations. That is
  the design the base spec already discloses, not a shortfall discovered late.

## 4. The quality gates flagged almost half the landed series

[limitations — 4. The quality gates flagged almos — part 1 of 2]

**672 series** are gated: **357 `ok`, 313 `flagged`, 2 `empty`**. `flagged` does not mean unusable — it
means a rule fired and the reason travels with the series into the base and the registry. The two empty
series are Eritrea's and Somalia's CPI in the donor panel, which the source has no data for.

## 4. The quality gates flagged almost half the landed series

[limitations — 4. The quality gates flagged almos — part 2 of 2]

- **8 definition breaks** are annotated rather than removed: GDP rebasing (2014), the unemployment
  methodology change, the January-2025 CPI rebasing (C-27), and the FX regime breaks among them.

  confounder that no adjustment set in this registry closes (C-28).

## 7. Design C is permission to build, not a result

[limitations — 7. Design C is permission to build — part 1 of 2]

Stage 5's earlier `infeasible` verdict was a statement about the **donor pool**. Widened from 13 to **99
countries**, the pre-fit gate now passes `u5mr` on **3 of its 4** runnable windows, `gdp_growth` on 1 of 4
and `cpi_yoy` on **0 of 4**, under a strict-majority rollup that is declared rather than inferred
(S5-12). The pass carries its own warning: **a 99-donor simplex can fit almost any pre-period**, and in
the 13-donor run a single donor beat the fitted simplex. The gate is weaker evidence now than it was then
(C-59).

chunks.text:

## 8. Inference floors that no interval can hide

[limitations — 8. Inference floors that no interv — part 1 of 2]

- **36 clusters, 114 national months.** A wild-cluster bootstrap would be the fix for the state-clustered
  errors and is **not applied**; the spec declares it. - **A permutation null is not automatically a valid null.** Shuffling the dose across states within a
  month destroys the cross-state mean the state fixed effects already absorb. It returned p = 0.000 on a
  design whose own placebo was 63 % of the estimate (S6-07). The time-shift null is the one that decides a
  timing claim, and it is the one reported as decisive. - **Oster's δ is negative for both designs** (A: −1.53 with the control set flipping the estimate's sign;
  B: −44.0 with the controls moving it away from zero).
chunks.citation: limitations — 8. Inference floors that no interval can hide — docs/limitations.md (vintage 2026-10-18)

## 8. Inference floors that no interval can hide

[limitations — 8. Inference floors that no interv — part 2 of 2]

Oster's δ ≥ 1 cutoff does not apply, and the
  artifact says so rather than reporting a number that reads like a pass (S7-05). - **Rosenbaum bounds are not applicable** — continuous treatment, no matching — and are recorded as such
  with the reason. - **Four events.** The transition study's exhaustive placebo over 58 eligible months cannot produce a
  p-value below **1/59 = 0.017**, and the family-wise maximum is published because a reader looking at
  four estimates is looking at the largest of four.

chunks.title: limitations — 10. Measurement limits no design fixes
chunks.text:
What this project cannot say — the limitations, written before the findings

## 10. Measurement limits no design fixes

- **UCDP GED is a reported-events archive.** The reporting-divergence check is a guard, not a correction,
  and it cannot rule out that a change in what the archive records produced a change in the series.
- **The index has two anchor regimes:** 25 anchors, **18 at the fixed January-2000 anchor and 7 on the
  recorded fallback rule**. The fallback is disclosed per series in the base.
- **The dose is nominal, not per capita.** With state fixed effects the elasticity is invariant to a
  state-constant denominator (S6-06) — but that is an argument, not a measurement.
- **Flagged series stay flagged.** Passing a flagged series into a model is allowed; forgetting the flag
  is not, and the registry carries the status onto every card.

chunks.title: limitations — 11. Reproduction limits
chunks.text:
What this project cannot say — the limitations, written before the findings

## 11. Reproduction limits

- **`data/raw/` is gitignored** (redistribution constraints). A stranger with their own credentials can
  rebuild every aggregate; a stranger without them cannot.
- **`oagf.gov.ng`'s TLS certificate expired 2026-10-17.** The FAAC vintage cannot be re-landed here or in
  CI until the publisher renews it. Nothing is bypassed: disabling verification would make a dead source
  look green.
- **CI has no R.** The Stage 6, 7, 8 and 8b engines are skipped there, so CI verifies the committed
  artifacts against the rebuilt base rather than re-estimating. That is weaker than a local run and is
  labelled as such rather than passed off.
- **The verifiers need the `ds-general` Python**, not the system 3.14 interpreter (no `duckdb`).

**What is not claimed, in the vocabulary the project refuses:** no ranking of presidents, no scorecard,
no pooled tenure effect, no party comparison (two events against two events has no sampling
distribution), no causal verb without a named design, and no monthly causal statement from an annual
series.

## 4. Reproducing it, and the ordering trap

[registry — 4. Reproducing it, and the ordering t — part 2 of 2]

**The ordering trap.** `analysis/R/01_build_dags.R` writes the cards wholesale, which **resets the estimate
block**. That is deliberate — a card generator that preserved a block it does not understand would make the
registry un-rebuildable — but it means the assembler must run after the generator. Two checks catch a broken
ordering rather than letting it look green: `validate_artifacts.py` compares the index's counts against the
cards on disk, and `verify_registry.py` fails when a card that should carry a number does not.

## 1. The grid

[robustness — 1. The grid — part 2 of 3]

The design spec (§5.4) names eight axes. Four are live here; four are not, and the four dead ones are
declared with their reason rather than quietly dropped: **imputation handling** (no imputed value enters
either design — the dose is read only where `dose_status = observed`, the count series is never
interpolated, S6-05), **index anchor** (the designs use levels, so the anchor is a scaling constant the
fixed effects absorb), **donor pool** (Design C was never run), and **event window** (neither design is
an event study; the tenure design that would need one is not estimable at this sample size).

## 2. Design B is robust in sign, and the timing is its weak part

[robustness — 2. Design B is robust in sign, and  — part 1 of 5]

All **24 of 24** specifications are positive, and **all 24 intervals exclude zero**. The pre-registered
specification is the published one — +0.5181 (SE 0.1664, 95 % CI [+0.1919, +0.8443]) on 111 months — and
the grid reproduces Stage 6's artifact to 4.3e-12, so the curve is drawn around the published estimate
rather than a neighbour of it.

## 2. Design B is robust in sign, and the timing is its weak part

[robustness — 2. Design B is robust in sign, and  — part 2 of 5]

Across the grid the coefficient at h = 2 runs from **+0.3968** to **+2.3976**. Which choice moves it is
a claim about the grid, so it is computed from the fitted rows and published in the artifact
(`robustness.json` → `spread.design_b`) rather than typed here: holding the shock definition and the
window fixed, the range across the four covariate sets averages **0.4073** (mean of the six shock × window
cells); holding the covariate set and the window fixed, the gap between the two shock definitions averages
**0.7548** (mean of the twelve covariate-set × window cells).

## 2. Design B is robust in sign, and the timing is its weak part

[robustness — 2. Design B is robust in sign, and  — part 3 of 5]

So the *magnitude* is a choice — mostly the
shock definition, a three-month average being a smoother and therefore larger-coefficient regressor —
while the *sign* is not. The decomposition is a mean of within-cell ranges rather than one chosen pair,
because a single pair would make the claim depend on which pair was picked. Two checks say where the weakness is:
chunks.citation: robustness — 2. Design B is robust in sign, and the timing is its weak part — docs/robustness.md (vintage 2026-10-18)

## 2. Design B is robust in sign, and the timing is its weak part

[robustness — 2. Design B is robust in sign, and  — part 4 of 5]

- **In-time placebo: p = 0.0625.** The shock series shifted by each of 48 non-zero offsets and the
  preferred specification refitted: 3 of 48 alignments return an estimate at least as large as the true
  one (placebo estimates average |0.1911|, maximum |0.6446|, against the estimate's +0.5181). This does
  **not** clear 0.05. The sign is the robust claim; the claim that the response is *specific to a two-to-
  three-month lag* is weaker, and the placebo is the check that tests it.
- **HAC bandwidth:** SE 0.1723 / 0.1664 / 0.1609 at 6 / 12 / 18 lags. The interval's width is not a
  bandwidth artefact — it is the sample.
chunks.citation: robustness — 2. Design B is robust in sign, and the timing is its weak part — docs/robustness.md (vintage 2026-10-18)

## 2. Design B is robust in sign, and the timing is its weak part

[robustness — 2. Design B is robust in sign, and  — part 5 of 5]

Oster's delta is reported and **does not have its usual reading here**: β runs 0.4882 with no controls to
0.5181 with month dummies, i.e. the controls move the estimate *away* from zero, so δ = −44.04 and Oster's
"δ ≥ 1" cutoff does not apply. The bias-adjusted β\* at δ = 1 is 0.5299. Reporting a negative delta as if
it were a robustness certification would be a misuse of the statistic, so the artifact says which case
it is in.

| `dose_lag_months = 1` | 17 of 27 |
| `adjustment_set = state_fe` (no month effects) | 16 of 27 |

## 3. Design A is not robust, and that is the finding

[robustness — 3. Design A is not robust, and that — part 2 of 5]

The count is not the whole story in either direction, which is why the minority is published beside it:
6 of the 105 specifications sit **within ±0.02 of zero** (6 Design A, 0 Design B) — the band is declared in
`robustness.yml` rather than chosen after the fact — and outside it the split is 42 positive / 33 negative
for Design A. A specification that is numerically zero is reported as a near-zero cell, not absorbed into
the sign counts as if it were a direction.

## 3. Design A is not robust, and that is the finding

[robustness — 3. Design A is not robust, and that — part 3 of 5]

The one that matters most is the **dose lag**. With the dose lagged one month and state and month effects,
the estimate is negative in all three windows while the pre-registered same-month specification is
positive. A quantity whose sign depends on a one-month timing choice is not a direction. Two sensitivities sharpen it rather than rescue it:

## 3. Design A is not robust, and that is the finding

[robustness — 3. Design A is not robust, and that — part 4 of 5]

- **Leave-one-state-out (36 refits):** coefficients range [0.1234, 0.6254] around 0.4793 with **0** sign
  flips. The estimate is not carried by one state — but dropping the three oil-producing states named in
  the spec (Delta, Bayelsa, Rivers) raises it to **0.6663**, because those states carry most of the dose's
  variation (C-47). - **Oster delta on the linear analogue** (log(1 + fatalities), the only form with an R²): the control set
  **flips the sign of the estimate**, from −0.1023 without controls to +0.0882 with state and month
  effects. δ = −1.53 therefore has no attenuation reading; it is the amount of unobserved selection that
  would have to act *against* the observed controls to zero the estimate.

## 4. What this changes about Stage 6

[robustness — 4. What this changes about Stage 6 — part 2 of 3]

- **Design B stands** — with one bound added: its sign is invariant across the grid, its timing is not
  (placebo p = 0.0625), and its magnitude is a choice of shock definition. - **Design A's verdict gets sharper, not softer.** Stage 6 said *estimated, not identified* because the
  dose's post-fixed-effect variation is the oil price moving the derivation share. This stage adds that
  the sign is not even stable across the declared choices — which is the same underlying fact seen from
  another angle, and a stronger statement than a single specification and its placebo could support. **No cell of this grid identifies Design A**, and the grid cannot create variation the dose does not
  have.

## 5. Reproducing it

[robustness — 5. Reproducing it — part 2 of 3]

The verifier re-fits all 81 Design A PPML specifications with `statsmodels` (not `fixest`), all 24 local
projections, all 36 leave-one-state-out refits and all 48 placebo alignments, and recomputes the support
counts, the majority-flip rule, both Oster bounds, the HAC table and the spread decomposition — the last
from its own re-fitted coefficients rather than from the published rows, so a grid fitted on something
else is caught rather than the summary being checked against itself. Worst coefficient disagreement
observed: 6.5e-9; worst clustered-SE gap 0.85 %, against a stated 5 % allowance.

## 5. Reproducing it

[robustness — 5. Reproducing it — part 3 of 3]

The artifact carries the **fingerprint of the base it was fitted on** — `state_panel` `dd11d300f588`,
`faac_national_monthly` `0084ea1d7129`, `oil_series` `167ff0dce42d`, hashed by the queries in
`robustness.yml` — and the verifier re-hashes the base on disk before it compares anything. A curve drawn
against a base that has since moved is visible as a mismatch rather than as a plausible-looking
disagreement, which is the failure mode C-42, C-44 and C-49 all belong to.

chunks.text:
[Model card cpi_yoy__B — Headline inflation (y/y) — part 3 of 5]

What this design cannot rule out:
- FAAC and the exchange rate are downstream of the administration, so conditioning on them identifies a *direct* effect net of the fiscal and FX channel, not the total effect.
- Only ~26 annual observations and five administrations — the interval is wide by construction.
- Structural breaks (2014 rebasing, 2016 and 2023 regime changes) are not fully absorbed by trends.
- Oil is treated as exogenous to Nigerian policy, which the 2016 and 2020 episodes roughly support but do not prove.

- FAAC and the exchange rate are downstream of the administration, so conditioning on them identifies a *direct* effect net of the fiscal and FX channel, not the total effect.

- Oil is treated as exogenous to Nigerian policy, which the 2016 and 2020 episodes roughly support but do not prove.

chunks.text:
[Published result — Design A — part 1 of 3]

Published result for Design A — State dose-response DiD. State dose-response: does a larger federal allocation reduce conflict fatalities? Estimator: PPML (Poisson pseudo-maximum-likelihood), fixest::fepois. Estimand: ATT of a federal policy shift, with state exposure intensity as the dose. Status: estimated_not_identified. Result is card-level: true. Verdict rule: Reported as `identified` only if the lead-shift p-value is below 0.05 **and** the 24-month placebo estimate is smaller in magnitude than the estimated coefficient. Otherwise `estimated_not_identified`, with the failed check named. Fixed before the numbers were read. Failed checks: the lead-shift p-value is 0.133: 8 of 60 mis-timed doses return an estimate at least as large as the estimate itself
Headline: The largest response is +0.5460 (incidents).

chunks.title: What this corpus can and cannot answer
chunks.text:
[What this corpus can and cannot answer — part 1 of 2]

What this corpus can answer: The corpus can answer questions about the 12 catalogue outcomes, the three identification designs, the published results and their checks, the data's coverage and quality, the administration and shock tables, and why a question cannot be answered. It cannot answer forecast questions, questions about countries outside the donor panel, or anything requiring an estimate that was never fitted; those must refuse. An answer is assembled in this order: question, estimate_with_interval, identifying_assumption, what_it_cannot_rule_out, citation. Post-check: Every assembled answer is checked for an interval, an identifying assumption and at least one chunk citation. A response missing any of the three is replaced by the refusal template, whatever the model produced (R-04). Refusal template: "I don't have a model for that.
